definition: Covet means to desire enviously what belongs to another.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word covet. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know covet should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: My little brother covets my record player so openly that he has already cleared a shelf for it in his room.
You admire the neighbor's roses without wanting to dig them up — admiration asks for nothing, unlike covet.
Desire wants the thing itself; it stops short of covet, which wants the very one that belongs to someone else — and minds that it does.

To crave is to want something intensely — sleep, salt, adventure — with no owner anywhere in the picture. Covet fixes on a possession that already belongs to somebody else and minds who has it. A craving names a kind of thing; covet points at the one with an owner.

Envy is resenting that another person has something; you may feel it without wanting the thing itself at all. Covet adds the wanting to the resentment: envious desire aimed at taking that very possession for your own. Envy can sit and stew; covet starts making room.

To begrudge is to resent that someone has or enjoys something, and the feeling stops at resentment. Covet goes one step further: besides minding that they have it, you want that very thing for yourself. You can begrudge a rival's promotion without wanting the job at all.

The Latin root cupere, 'to desire,' reaches English only in disguise — the god Cupid, desire with a bow, and the bookish word cupidity, which you may meet elsewhere in this course. Covet itself fused into a single piece centuries ago, so there is no everyday relative to build from.
Covet means to desire enviously what belongs to another.
The duke coveted his neighbor's harbor for years, mapping its docks from a hilltop he pretended to visit for the view.
Covet is not simple wanting: it is envious desire aimed at what belongs to someone else — wanting not just such a thing, but that one, the one with an owner.
The tenth commandment uses exactly this word, which tells you how old the itch is.
Covet carries the old commandment's shadow: envious desire for what is another's.
Want and crave are innocent by comparison; envy resents the owner but may not want the thing.
Use covet when the wanting fixes on someone else's particular possession — the corner office, not corner offices.
